changed_views: AI-for-science progress should be segmented by how much the field can be searched with consistency checks versus how much it needs new experimental evidence.
Opaque formal proof is not the only plausible AI math future; the same systems may also produce compressed, human-usable explanations.
follow_ups: Track Google DeepMind BlueShift outputs for concrete evidence of AI-assisted theoretical physics or math discovery.
Watch whether new AI math results are accompanied by human-interpretable ideas or only formal certificates.

signals.claim: AI science systems may be most useful when sparse empirical constraints leave only a small theory tree to search.
signals.evidence: Brown says general relativity was unusually discoverable from little empirical input; many LLMs could explore finite branches such as equivalence principle variants, but this works only when consistency and known limits narrow the space.

signals.claim: Fields with many internally consistent theories will still need experiments to prune AI-generated candidates.
signals.evidence: Brown contrasts string theory's hope that consistency uniquely selects a gravity theory with condensed matter, where experiments are often needed to choose among many possible theories.

signals.claim: Brown is more optimistic that LLM proof systems will also become strong explainers, not just opaque proof generators.
signals.evidence: He cites recent AI math examples where the machine-produced idea was human-interpretable and then reused by mathematicians, arguing against the default 'billion-line Lean' pessimism.

signals.claim: LLMs' patience may be a genuine research advantage on conjectures humans avoid because they look low-probability.
signals.evidence: Brown says models can keep pushing at paths that humans would treat as wasted effort, using the unit distance conjecture as an example where willingness to attack a presumed-true conjecture mattered.

summary: Mostly a general-relativity lecture, but the final section has useful signal on where AI science systems may and may not help: parallel LLMs look more promising when the theory search tree is small, consistency checks are strong, and human interpretation remains possible.
why_it_matters: The discussion is a concrete scientist's view on AI-assisted theoretical discovery. It argues that parallel model search is not a universal substitute for experiments, but could be powerful in constrained theory spaces and in translating hard proofs into human-comprehensible ideas.
